hypothesis: If chromosome numbers of germ-nuclei mostly lie between six and sixteen, with few below six and fewer still above sixteen, then across plant species the haploid (gametic) number n has most of its mass in 6 <= n <= 16, a small lower tail (n < 6) and a still smaller upper tail (n > 16).
pass_criterion: Pre-registered. Data: the Chromosome Counts Database (CCDB, Rice et al. 2015), 'statistics' API output (one row per resolved species name with the median gametophytic/sporophytic counts) retrieved per major group (Angiosperms, Gymnosperms, Pteridophytes, Bryophytes) in CSV. One n per species: the median resolved gametophytic count; where only a sporophytic (2n) count is given, n = 2n/2; species with no usable count excluded. SUPPORTS if all three hold: (a) at least 70% of species have 6 <= n <= 16; (b) fewer than 15% have n < 6; (c) the share with n > 16 is smaller than the share with n < 6.
fail_criterion: Pre-registered. REFUTES if any holds: fewer than 50% of species have 6 <= n <= 16; the share with n > 16 is >= the share with n < 6; or the share with n > 16 is >= 15%. MIXED otherwise. INCONCLUSIVE (data-unavailable) if the API cannot be read; INCONCLUSIVE (underpowered) if fewer than 1000 species have a usable n.
interpretation: 'Germ-nuclei' chromosome number is the reduced (haploid, gametic) number n. Thompson wrote before polyploidy was understood; using the median count per species keeps polyploid cytotypes within a species from counting as extra species. The database covers land plants only, so this decides the plant half of the claim ('plants and animals'); the animal half is not tested. 'Few' and 'fewer still' are read as the two tails of the distribution with the lower tail larger than the upper. Follows the swarm thread's draft plan with the data access route specified.

datasets.name: Chromosome Counts Database (CCDB, Rice et al. 2015), 'statistics' API output per major plant group (one row per resolved species name with minimum, median and maximum count)
datasets.license: not stated on the site; community database, cite the paper

method: fetch.py downloads four CSV files (2.7 MB). analysis.py takes the median count per resolved species name, confirms on six reference species (Arabidopsis n=5, maize 10, wheat 21, rice 12, Scots pine 12, silver fir 12) that the column is at the haploid level, drops duplicates and non-numeric rows, and computes the shares of species with n < 6, 6 <= n <= 16 and n > 16, overall and by major group. The pre-registered rule is applied.

measured.unit: share of plant species with haploid number n > 16 (claim: 'fewer still' than the share with n < 6, which is given in extra)
measured.uncertainty: binomial standard error below 0.002 at this sample size

caveats: Thompson's central range is roughly right (64% of species have 6 <= n <= 16, mode n = 9), but the upper tail is 20 times larger than the lower tail (34% above 16 versus 1.7% below 6), the opposite of 'fewer still have more than sixteen': polyploidy, unknown in 1917, puts a third of angiosperms and 96% of ferns above 16.
Plants only; the animal half of the claim is untested here (animal karyotype compilations were not pursued in this batch).
The CCDB is a compilation of published counts with uneven taxonomic coverage; the median per species name hides within-species cytotype variation, which is the intended treatment of polyploid races.
Species with only a sporophytic count: the CCDB statistics service reports counts at the gametophytic level (confirmed on reference species), so no halving was applied.
